case_study_insert.main_stem: Redmoor Abrasives (RMA) is a public limited company in the industrial abrasives sector, manufacturing resin-bond grinding wheels and cutting discs for steel fabrication plants, employing a workforce of 140. Founded in 1998 by Marek Nowak, the business operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership and is based in Łódź, Poland. RMA plans to invest $1,600,000 in a new high-speed pressing and curing line, financed by a $1,000,000 share issue and $600,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $528,000 a year, a variable cost of $13.00 a unit and a selling price of $24.00, and currently produces 96,000 units a year. RMA faces a serious HR problem: absenteeism has reached 8.4% and labour turnover among press operators is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The grinding-wheel line produced 24,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.7% a year ago. On-time delivery stands at 95.1%. Abrasive grit waste fell from 6.4% to 4.1% of input mass. Wheels are currently wrapped in single-use plastic; trials of ribbed cardboard eco-packaging show transit damage fell 18%. A market research survey of 320 factory maintenance managers found that 68% specify open-web wheels for wet grinding and 55% would accept a 3% price increase for batch-tested wheels. A training needs analysis shows 22 of 140 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new press; off-the-job courses at the local college cost $700 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Redmoor Abrasives as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.25% to 6.00%, the fourth rise this year, increasing repayment costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $13.00 to $13.78 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills across heavy industry. (3) Aluminium oxide and resin input costs have risen 10.7% year-on-year, industrial inflation is running at 7.4%, and construction activity grew 2.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: RMA plans to finance part of its pressing-line expansion with a share issue. Explain two advantages for RMA of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the share issue.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs RMA no dividends, issue costs or underwriting fees, so the $600,000 stays inside the business and protects earnings per share for existing shareholders. This matters while RMA carries fixed costs of $528,000 a year: every dollar of profit reinvested rather than paid out can absorb the 10.7% rise in aluminium oxide and resin input costs without diluting headline earnings for the 2027 reporting year.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids issuing new shares, which would dilute the control and voting power of Marek Nowak and the founding shareholder group in the public limited company. Using retained profit instead of selling $600,000 of equity keeps decision-making with current owners, avoids the effort and expense of a prospectus and shareholder meetings, and signals to the market that the board is confident the new line will generate its own returns without fresh capital. It also reassures investors that RMA's growth story is equity-financed rather than debt-driven, protecting the share price that funded the other $1,000,000 of the programme.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Redmoor Abrasives and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: RMA is launching its batch-tested grinding wheel range. Consider a stand at a national metal fabrication exhibition, advertising in an industrial abrasives trade magazine, or local radio sponsorship. Which should RMA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National fabrication exhibition stand: A stand would concentrate hundreds of factory maintenance managers and buyers in one hall, ideal for live grinding demonstrations and securing batch orders from the 55% of the 320 surveyed managers willing to accept a 3% price increase for tested wheels. However, exhibition fees, build costs, freighting of machine tools and staffing over two or three days are heavy for a business committing $1,600,000 to a new line, and attendance is limited to visitors who may already have preferred suppliers.

Industrial trade magazine advertising: Full-page technical features in fabrication and machining magazines reach professional readers with credible surroundings and long shelf life, reaching remote plants far beyond Łódź. Drawbacks are slower production lead times, difficulty proving which enquiries the advertising generated, and wastage where circulation extends to maintenance teams who do not specify abrasives.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheap, fast to launch and excellent for recruitment and local brand warmth around the Łódź factory. Its reach, however, is geographically narrow and hard to target at procurement decision-makers across Poland, so it cannot build the national specification base RMA needs to justify a 96,000-unit annual output.

Recommendation: RMA should choose the national fabrication exhibition stand. It puts the tested batch certification story directly in front of the 68% who specify open-web wheels and the 55% premium-accepting buyers identified in its research, creates memorable face-to-face demonstrations, and generates trial orders measurably. Trade magazine advertising is rejected as too weak on immediacy and accountability for a launch; local radio is rejected as far too narrow for a national industrial customer base; exhibition costs should be offset by pre-booked appointments and follow-up calls to firms that request batch test certificates at the stand.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of RMA with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of RMA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade magazine advertising and local radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: RMA's absenteeism has reached 8.4% and labour turnover among press operators is rising. Explain two benefits for RMA of introducing a bonus scheme for press operators.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bonus tied to attendance and output gives press operators a direct financial reason to show up for every shift, attacking the 8.4% absenteeism that is disrupting the new high-speed line. Reliable attendance stabilises the curing schedule, protects the 2.2% defect rate achieved this quarter, and keeps on-time delivery at 95.1% for fabrication plants that penalise late shipments.

Point 2: Bonuses reward contribution visibly and satisfy the esteem needs (Maslow) and hygiene factors (Herzberg) that pay alone cannot. For a workforce of 140 with rising turnover among press operators, a clear bonus structure raises commitment, reduces the indirect costs of covering absent shifts and rehiring, and makes RMA more attractive to skilled recruits — critical while 22 staff still need on-the-job training and each leaver slows the ramp-up of the $1,600,000 pressing and curing investment. Lower absenteeism also trims the overtime premium required to cover missing press operators, easing pressure on the $528,000 fixed-cost base.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RMA's attendance, turnover, defect and expansion data.

questions.question_text: RMA wants to motivate all 140 employees. Consider an attendance bonus or profit sharing. Which should RMA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Attendance bonus: A bonus paid for meeting agreed attendance and punctuality targets directly attacks RMA's 8.4% absenteeism among press operators. It is immediate, easy to understand, and cheap to administer on top of existing wages; it rewards the specific behaviour RMA needs and can be withdrawn or tightened as the new line stabilises. Its limits are that it pays for presence rather than effort, may irritate genuinely ill staff, and does nothing directly to lift creativity, waste reduction or batch quality once attendance stabilises.

Profit sharing: Sharing a portion of annual profits with all 140 employees builds a common financial interest in RMA's success, can improve industrial relations, and suits a public limited company wanting to align staff with shareholders. However, payouts are distant, hard for workers to connect to their own daily behaviour, hostage to year-end profit swings driven by input-cost inflation of 10.7%, and dilute motivation when profits dip despite individual effort — precisely the situation RMA faces while the new line ramps up.

Decision: RMA should choose the attendance bonus as its primary motivational tool for the next 12 to 18 months. It targets the measurable 8.4% absenteeism that is disrupting commissioning of the new line, delivers fast, legible rewards on the shop floor, and is affordable while fixed costs of $528,000 a year and the share issue must be safeguarded. Profit sharing is rejected as too diffuse and too dependent on whole-company profit to change operator behaviour in the short term; once attendance normalises, RMA can layer a modest profit-sharing pool on top to sustain engagement beyond the commissioning phase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivational methods with limited application to RMA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both motivational methods in the context of RMA.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both motivational methods in the context of RMA with a well-justified decision covering immediacy, cost, fairness and shareholder interests.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RMA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $528,000 ÷ ($24.00 − $13.00) = $528,000 ÷ $11.00 = 48,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 48,000 units a year.
Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: 96,000 units − 48,000 units = 48,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 48,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RMA's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 48,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 96,000 units to confirm the wheel line is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 48,000 units, and use that cushion to justify loading the new curing line harder rather than booking overtime recklessly.
2. Contribution per unit of $11.00 lets RMA model discounting for large fabrication contracts, for example cutting 8% to $22.08 would leave contribution of about $9.08, letting managers judge whether the extra volume still covers the $528,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $528,000 and the 48,000-unit break-even helps managers set monthly volume targets for the sales team and identify when to throttle output of, for example, cutting discs if demand slows.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($528,000 ÷ 96,000 units + $13.00 = $18.50 a unit) to benchmark quarter against quarter, pinpoint waste behind the 4.1% grit waste and 2.2% defect rate, and test whether supplier renegotiation amid the 10.7% input-cost inflation protects the $11.00 contribution before prices must rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 48,000 units | (ii) margin of safety = 48,000 units | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: the 48,000-unit cushion against 96,000-unit output; discount modelling on the $11.00 contribution; volume targeting for the new curing line; and unit-cost benchmarking at $18.50 to attack grit waste and the 2.2% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RMA's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RMA's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.70 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.05 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.09 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $260,000 inventories + $300,000 trade receivables + $120,000 cash = $680,000; 2025 current assets = $240,000 + $350,000 + $170,000 = $760,000. 2024 = $680,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.70; 2025 = $760,000 ÷ $475,000 = 1.60. Quick cover 2024 = ($680,000 − $260,000) ÷ $400,000 = $420,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.05; 2025 = ($760,000 − $240,000) ÷ $475,000 = $520,000 ÷ $475,000 = 1.09.

Evaluation: Liquidity remains comfortable in absolute terms but the headline trend is slightly worse while the underlying quality of the numbers is better. Short-term cover eased from 1.70 to 1.60 because current liabilities grew from $400,000 to $475,000 to part-fund the new line, yet total assets and cash both rose — cash is up from $120,000 to $170,000. Inventories actually fell from $260,000 to $240,000, improvements that show disciplined stock control on a fast-moving product line, while quick cover strengthened from 1.05 to 1.09, so RMA depends less on selling grit-heavy stock to pay short-term creditors. The caution is receivables rising to $350,000 from $300,000; if fabrication customers stretch payment terms by even a month, short-term cover would tighten toward the 1.3 range while a $1,600,000 line still needs consistent volume to pay back.

Conclusion: RMA's financial position has broadly improved in quality even though the headline short-term cover dipped from 1.70 to 1.60. Quick cover (1.05 to 1.09) and a lower inventory burden show stronger, more dependable liquidity, and cash grew by $50,000. The rise in trade receivables and the heavier liability base mean the position is not fully comfortable, so RMA should tighten credit control and keep the curing line at high utilisation to ensure the $600,000 retained profit portion of the expansion continues to reward shareholders.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether RMA's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RMA of switching its grinding wheels to ribbed cardboard eco-packaging.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-packaging fits the 18% reduction in transit damage recorded in RMA's own wrapping trials and supports the premium segment — the 55% of maintenance managers willing to accept a 3% price increase for batch-tested wheels. Marketing the switch allows RMA to charge that premium with a clear conscience story, win preferred-supplier status with fabrication plants pursuing their own sustainability targets, and reduce the 4.1% grit waste problem by keeping products intact through transport to Łódź distribution points.

Disadvantage: Cardboard packing costs more per unit than single-use plastic film and may need redesigning for the heaviest resin-bond disc sizes, pushing the effective variable cost above the $13.00 assumption and squeezing the $11.00 contribution per unit unless RMA negotiates the full 3% premium they signalled. Any failure in damp warehouses — softer packs, torn corners during hydration of resin — would also raise the current 2.2% defect-related complaints and dent the 95.1% on-time delivery promise that RMA's buyers expect during wet-grinding seasons.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to RMA's packaging trials, research data, costs and delivery record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.00%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 10.7% rise in input costs will affect RMA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.25% to 6.00%): RMA funded its $1,600,000 expansion through a $1,000,000 share issue and $600,000 retained profit, not a bank loan, so the direct repayment effect of the 0.75 percentage point rise is nil today — no variable-rate loan sits on its books. If RMA later chose to fund a phase-two press with debt, 0.75% would cost 0.75% × $1,600,000 = $12,000 a year (0.0075 × $1,600,000), but that is optional, not current, and the share issue shields shareholders and cash flow from rate shocks right now. The rise may also temper borrowing among fabrication customers, slowing orders, and will lift any future lease costs for the planned second kiln or curing oven.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.78 per hour from April 2026): With a workforce of 140, most of whom are hourly press and packing operatives, the rise is unavoidable. The insert states no hours worked and no pay decomposition, so no annual wage total can be honestly invented; the honest test is productivity: 96,000 units ÷ 140 staff ≈ 686 units per worker a year. If productivity holds at that level and RMA passes the attendance bonus carefully, the rise is absorbable; if not, unit labour cost climbs, the $11.00 contribution shrinks, and the 8.4% absenteeism problem becomes costlier to cover.

Input cost inflation (10.7% aluminium oxide and resin): RMA's $13.00 variable cost is heavily driven by abrasive grains and bonding resins, though the insert never decomposes it, so only an illustrative bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 10.7% it would add 10.7% × $13.00 = $1.39 per unit (0.107 × $13.00 = $1.39); at 96,000 units a year that is about $133,440 (96,000 × $1.39). Even a milder illustrative $1.00 per unit would strip about $96,000 a year. Unlike interest, this compounds on every unit made and sold, and unlike wages, it rises regardless of headcount control; RMA can recover part of it only through the 3% premium the 55% premium-accepting buyers will tolerate and through renegotiating supply contracts.

Conclusion: The 10.7% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact, removing up to roughly $133,000 a year if fully passed through the $13.00 variable cost and hitting every one of the 96,000 units — directly eroding the $11.00 contribution that underpins both dividends and the expansion case. The minimum wage rise is second, manageable through attendance discipline and productivity near 686 units per worker; the 6.00% base-rate rise is a clear third for RMA because its $1,600,000 programme is share-issue and retained-profit financed. RMA should lock multi-year resin supply contracts, accelerate the 18% cardboard damage saving, and use batch-testing certification to enforce the 3% premium before absorbing any further cost.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to RMA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on RMA's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of RMA with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
